before.content_html:
Where Fibres Come From

All textiles begin with a fibre — a fine, hair-like strand that is spun into yarn and woven, knitted or bonded into fabric. Fibres fall into two broad families: natural (sourced from plants and animals) and synthetic (manufactured from chemicals, usually derived from crude oil). Understanding the origin of each fibre is essential because it directly determines the fibre's properties and its environmental impact.

Natural Fibres

Cotton is a cellulose fibre harvested from the seed pod of the cotton plant, grown in warm climates such as India, the USA and China. It is soft, comfortable against the skin, strong when wet and highly absorbent — making it ideal for T-shirts, towels and bed linen. Cotton is breathable but creases easily and can shrink if washed at high temperatures.

Wool is a protein fibre shorn from sheep (and other animals such as alpacas and goats for specialist wools). It is naturally warm because the crimped fibre traps air pockets, and it has excellent moisture management — absorbing up to 30% of its own weight in water vapour without feeling wet. Wool is used for knitwear, suits and blankets. It requires careful washing because it felts if agitated in hot water.

Silk is a continuous protein filament produced by the silkworm (Bombyx mori) as it spins its cocoon. Silk is exceptionally smooth, lustrous and strong for its weight. It drapes beautifully and is used for luxury garments, scarves and linings. Silk is expensive because production is labour-intensive: the cocoons must be unreeled by hand in hot water to preserve the continuous filament.

Linen is made from the stem fibres of the flax plant. It is one of the oldest textile fibres known to humanity. Linen is stronger than cotton, highly absorbent, and becomes softer and more lustrous with washing. It is cool to wear in summer but creases severely. Linen is used for shirts, trousers, table linen and home furnishings.

Key Fact

Natural plant fibres (cotton, linen) are made of cellulose; natural animal fibres (wool, silk) are made of protein. This distinction matters: cellulose fibres generally absorb moisture well, while protein fibres naturally resist fire and can absorb moisture vapour without feeling damp.

Synthetic Fibres

Synthetic fibres are manufactured by extruding a liquid polymer through tiny holes called spinnerets to produce continuous filaments. The raw material is almost always derived from crude oil, a non-renewable petrochemical resource.

Polyester is the world's most widely produced synthetic fibre. It is strong, durable, wrinkle-resistant and dries very quickly — properties that make it ideal for sportswear, fleece jackets and workwear. Polyester does not absorb moisture well, which can make it feel clammy next to the skin during exercise, though modern microfibre versions draw sweat away by capillary action.

Nylon (polyamide) was the first fully synthetic fibre, developed in the 1930s. It is exceptionally strong and abrasion-resistant, making it popular for tights, hosiery, ropes, parachutes and backpack fabrics. Nylon is lightweight and recovers well from stretching, but like polyester it absorbs little moisture and can build up static charge.

Acrylic is often used as a cheaper substitute for wool because it is soft, lightweight and warm. Acrylic is resistant to sunlight degradation, making it useful for outdoor fabrics and upholstery. However, it pills readily (small balls of fibre form on the surface), it melts rather than burns and it is not biodegradable.

Elastane (brand name Lycra) is a polyurethane-based fibre capable of stretching to five to seven times its original length and recovering fully (some sources cite up to 8×; 5–6× is the most commonly cited figure) and recovering fully. Even a small percentage added to a fabric (2–5%) gives it significant stretch and recovery. Elastane is used in swimwear, cycling shorts, sportswear and stretch denim.

The manufacturing process is called melt spinning (for polyester and nylon) or wet spinning (for acrylic). In melt spinning, the polymer chips are melted and forced through a spinneret. The fine streams of polymer solidify in cool air to form continuous filaments, which are then drawn (stretched) under tension to align the polymer chains — this increases strength and reduces extensibility. Multiple filaments are bundled into a yarn. Filament yarns are smooth and lustrous; filaments can also be cut into short lengths called staple fibres to mimic the texture of natural fibres when spun.

Blended and Mixed Fibres

A blended fibre combines two or more fibre types in the same yarn to combine the best properties of each. The most common example is polycotton (typically 65% polyester, 35% cotton): polyester contributes durability, quick drying and wrinkle resistance; cotton contributes softness, breathability and comfort. Polycotton is used for school shirts, bed sheets and workwear.

A mixed fabric uses different fibres in the warp and weft yarns (the threads running lengthways and widthways in a woven fabric) rather than blending them in the same yarn. The result is a fabric with different properties in each direction. Blending and mixing allow designers to engineer performance characteristics that no single fibre could provide alone.

Key Fact

Blends are created to improve performance (e.g. stretch + strength), reduce cost (synthetic fibres are cheaper than silk or wool), and balance care requirements (machine-washable wool blends are easier to maintain than 100% wool). Always link each fibre in the blend to a specific benefit it contributes.

Ecological and Social Footprint of Fibre Production

No fibre is entirely without environmental or social impact. Cotton is the world's most pesticide-intensive crop — conventional cotton production uses roughly 6% of the world's pesticides despite occupying only 2.4% of its farmland. It also requires enormous volumes of water: it takes approximately 10,000 litres of water to produce 1 kilogram of cotton. Organic cotton avoids synthetic pesticides but yields less per hectare and is more expensive.

Synthetic fibres such as polyester and nylon depend on crude oil, a finite, non-renewable resource. Their production involves energy-intensive chemical processes and releases greenhouse gases. Crucially, synthetic fabrics shed microplastics — tiny plastic fragments — every time they are washed. These particles pass through wastewater treatment systems into rivers and oceans, entering the food chain. A single wash of a fleece jacket can release more than 700,000 microplastic fibres.

The social footprint of fibre production includes working conditions in cotton-farming communities (where pesticide exposure causes health problems), and in textile mills where low wages, long hours and poor safety standards remain common concerns in some producing countries. Fair trade certification schemes and industry codes of conduct aim to improve conditions, but enforcement is patchy across global supply chains.

One response to the environmental cost of virgin synthetic fibre is recycled polyester (rPET), made by melting down plastic bottles or post-consumer textile waste and extruding new filaments. Producing rPET uses approximately 59% less energy than virgin polyester. Many sportswear brands now use rPET extensively in their ranges. However, recycled synthetics still shed microplastics, and the sorting, cleaning and reprocessing of mixed-fibre garments remains technically challenging, so not all post-consumer textile waste can currently be recycled back into fibre.

before.content_html:
Applying Colour: Dyeing

Colour can be applied to textiles at several stages of production: to the raw fibre before spinning (called stock dyeing), to the spun yarn before weaving or knitting (yarn dyeing, which allows multicoloured woven patterns), or to the finished fabric (piece dyeing, the most common industrial method). The dye must form a chemical or physical bond with the fibre for the colour to be permanent. Different fibre types require different classes of dye: reactive dyes bond chemically with cellulose fibres (cotton, linen); acid dyes are used for protein fibres (wool, silk); disperse dyes are used for polyester and acetate, which must be dyed under high temperature and pressure because the dye molecules have to physically enter the fibre.

Resist dyeing techniques create patterns by preventing dye from reaching certain areas. Batik uses hot wax applied to fabric to resist the dye; where the wax is, the original colour is preserved. After dyeing, the wax is removed (by boiling or scraping), revealing the undyed pattern. Batik originated in Java and is used to create distinctive crackle-effect patterns in fashion and furnishing fabrics. Tie-dye creates patterns by tying or folding the fabric tightly before immersing it in dye; the bound areas resist penetration.

Printing Methods

Printing applies colour in a controlled pattern to the surface of a fabric, rather than immersing the whole cloth in dye. The most commercially important methods are:

  • Block printing — the oldest textile printing technique. A carved wooden or lino block is coated with dye paste and pressed firmly onto the fabric. Each colour requires a separate block, and the process is slow and labour-intensive, giving each print a handmade quality. Block printing is used for craft production and high-end artisan fabrics but is impractical for mass production.
  • Screen printing (flat bed and rotary) — a fine mesh screen stretched over a frame is coated with a light-sensitive emulsion. A photographic positive of the design is laid on the screen and exposed to UV light; where the light falls, the emulsion hardens. Where the design blocks light, the emulsion washes away, leaving open mesh. Dye paste is forced through the open mesh onto the fabric. One screen is made per colour. Flat-bed screen printing is used for shorter runs; rotary screen printing (cylindrical screens rotating around the moving fabric) is used for very high-volume production.
  • Digital (inkjet) printing — a digital image file is printed directly onto treated fabric using modified inkjet heads that deposit reactive or pigment inks. There is no minimum print run, so individual bespoke designs or short runs are economical. Digital printing can reproduce photographic-quality images with unlimited colours in one pass. It produces less dye waste than screen printing but is slower and more expensive per metre for very large runs.
  • Sublimation printing — a specialised digital printing method used specifically for white polyester fabrics. The design is first printed onto transfer paper using sublimation inks. The paper is then pressed onto the polyester fabric under high heat (~200 °C): the ink sublimes (converts directly from solid to gas) and the gas molecules diffuse into the polyester fibre, where they re-solidify permanently. The result is a vibrant, wash-resistant print with no hand feel (no ink layer on the surface). Used extensively for sportswear, cycling kit and soft signage.
Key Fact

Digital printing requires no screens and no minimum print run, making it ideal for personalised or short-run production. Sublimation printing produces prints with no surface layer (the ink is inside the fibre), so the fabric retains its original handle and the print cannot crack or peel — unlike screen-printed plastisol inks.

Surface Decoration

Beyond printing, textiles can be decorated using added materials and stitching:

  • Embroidery — decorative stitching worked onto a base fabric using a needle and thread. Traditional hand embroidery is very slow and is reserved for bespoke and couture work. Industrial machine embroidery uses computerised multi-head embroidery machines that simultaneously stitch the same design on dozens of garments; used for logos on workwear, caps and school uniform. The design is created as a digitised stitch file.
  • Appliqué — pieces of fabric are cut out and stitched onto a base fabric to create a layered, dimensional design. The applied fabric can be plain, printed or itself embroidered. Appliqué is used in quilting, children's clothing and soft furnishings. Industrial versions use bonded appliqué (iron-on adhesive backing) for speed.
  • Quilting — two or more layers of fabric are stitched together, usually with a layer of wadding (padding) in between, through a grid or decorative pattern of stitching. The stitching compresses the layers in a pattern, creating a textured, three-dimensional surface. Quilting provides warmth (the wadding traps air) and is used in bedding, padded jackets and upholstery.

Embroidery, appliqué and quilting each suit different skill levels and project scales. Embroidery requires only a needle, thread and fabric, making it accessible and low-cost; it allows fine detail but is slow by hand — even a small motif takes considerable time. Appliqué is quicker for bold, graphic shapes: cut a piece, bond it with iron-on adhesive, then stitch around the edge — the result is colourful and durable. Quilting is best chosen when both warmth and decoration are needed together, such as a padded wall hanging or cushion cover, because the wadding adds function as well as texture. For most school-level textile projects, appliqué or hand embroidery are the most practical starting points; quilting suits more experienced makers who can manage three fabric layers accurately.

Finishes and Treatments

After construction (or after dyeing), fabrics are frequently given a finish to improve their functional or aesthetic properties. Key finishes include:

  • Waterproofing / Durable Water Repellent (DWR) — a chemical coating applied to the fabric surface causes water droplets to bead up and roll off rather than soaking in. Common on outdoor jackets, tents and umbrellas. DWR coatings wear off with use and washing and must be reapplied.
  • Flame-retardant finish — a chemical treatment that reduces the flammability of the fabric by releasing non-combustible gases or forming a char layer when the fabric is exposed to flame. Legally required for children's nightwear (UK Night Clothes Safety Regulations), upholstered furniture and contract (public building) soft furnishings.
  • Stain-resistant finish — a fluorocarbon or silicone coating reduces the surface energy of the fibres, causing liquids to bead on the surface before they can be absorbed. Used on school ties, table linen and upholstery. The finish makes the fabric easier to clean but must be reapplied periodically.
  • Crease-resistant (easy care) finish — a resin applied to cotton or linen fabrics cross-links the cellulose fibres at the molecular level, preventing the hydrogen bonds that cause creasing from forming when the fabric is wet or worn. This makes the fabric easier to iron and helps garments retain their pressed shape. A trade-off is slightly reduced strength and absorbency.
  • Brushing (raising) — a mechanical finish in which the fabric surface is passed over rollers covered with fine wire hooks that lift fibres into a soft nap. Brushed cotton (flannelette) and fleece fabrics are examples; brushing improves warmth by trapping more air in the raised surface.
Key Fact

A flame-retardant finish is a legal requirement for children's nightwear in the UK, not just an optional performance upgrade. Always mention specific legislation when discussing this finish in an exam — it demonstrates awareness that design decisions are governed by regulation as well as aesthetics.

Smart and Technical Textiles

Smart textiles respond to changes in the environment and can actively adapt their properties. Technical textiles are engineered for high-performance applications rather than appearance:

  • Gore-Tex — a laminated membrane bonded to an outer fabric. The membrane contains over 1.4 billion microscopic pores per square centimetre: large enough to let water vapour (sweat) pass outwards but too small to let liquid water droplets in from the outside. This gives Gore-Tex its waterproof-yet-breathable properties. Used in hiking jackets, ski wear and surgical gowns.
  • Conductive (e-textiles) — yarns incorporating metal-coated fibres or fine stainless steel threads can carry electrical current, allowing electronic components such as sensors, LEDs or heating elements to be integrated directly into a garment. Applications include heated motorcycle gloves, ECG monitoring shirts and wearable fitness trackers.
  • Thermochromic textiles — thermochromic textiles contain pigments (usually microencapsulated leuco dyes) that change colour at a specific temperature. Applications include novelty T-shirts, swimwear that changes colour in warm water, and neonatal medical garments where a colour change signals that a baby's temperature has dropped below a safe threshold.
  • Phase-change materials (PCMs) — microcapsules of wax embedded in fibre or applied to fabric absorb heat as they melt (during activity, slowing overheating) and release heat as they re-solidify (during rest, slowing cooling). PCMs are used in high-performance base layers for mountaineering and military applications.

Smart and e-textile technologies face several barriers to mass-market adoption. Electronic components integrated into garments must withstand repeated washing, bending, sweat and mechanical stress — conditions that degrade conventional electronics rapidly. Data privacy is a concern when biometric garments continuously monitor the wearer. Costs remain high because smart textiles are often produced in small volumes with specialised manufacturing processes. And at end of life, garments mixing electronic components with textiles are very difficult to separate for recycling. Despite these challenges, the global smart textiles market is growing rapidly, driven by demand from healthcare, defence and sportswear sectors.

before.exam_tip_html: When asked to compare printing methods, structure your comparison around three key variables: speed/volume suitability, cost (set-up vs. per-unit), and quality/versatility. For example: 'Screen printing has a high set-up cost (one screen per colour) but a very low cost per metre for long runs, making it ideal for mass production. Digital printing has no set-up cost and can reproduce unlimited colours, making it better for short runs or personalised items.' This paired structure — one advantage, one limitation per method — is exactly what the mark scheme rewards at 6 and 8 marks.

before.content_html:
Scales of Production for Textile Products

Textile and clothing manufacture occurs across a wide spectrum of production scales, from a designer making a single couture piece to a factory producing millions of identical garments per year. Understanding the differences between these scales is essential for evaluating cost, quality control, flexibility and environmental impact:

  • One-off (bespoke) production — a single item made entirely to the client's individual specification. A tailor-made suit or a bespoke wedding dress are examples. Each stage is performed by a skilled craftsperson; quality is high and highly personal, but unit cost is very high and production is very slow. There is no economy of scale.
  • Batch production — a set quantity of identical items is produced together, then the production line is reconfigured for a different product. A fashion brand producing 500 units of a particular jacket style uses batch production. Set-up costs are spread across the batch, lowering unit cost compared with one-off production. Machinery is set up specifically for that batch, then changed over — producing downtime between batches.
  • Mass (continuous flow) production — very large quantities of identical products are produced continuously, with workers and machines each performing one specialist task in a moving production line. T-shirts, socks and school uniform are mass-produced. Unit costs are very low due to economies of scale, but there is very little flexibility: retooling for a different product is expensive and slow. Quality control relies on statistical sampling at key stages.
  • Just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing — a lean production system in which materials and components arrive at the production line exactly when needed, minimising the warehouse storage of stock. Used by fast fashion brands such as Zara, which replenishes store ranges weekly. JIT reduces storage costs but relies on a highly reliable, geographically close supply chain — disruptions such as transport delays can halt production.
Key Fact

The concept of economies of scale explains why mass-produced T-shirts can retail for a few pounds while a bespoke tailored jacket costs hundreds: in mass production, the fixed costs (machinery, factory, management) are divided between millions of items, making each one very cheap to produce.

Sustainability and the 6Rs Applied to Textiles

The textile and fashion industries are among the most environmentally damaging on Earth, responsible for approximately 10% of global carbon emissions and 20% of industrial water pollution. The 6Rs framework — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Rethink, Refuse and Repair — provides a structure for evaluating and improving sustainability at every stage of the textile product life cycle:

  • Reduce — using less material at the design stage through efficient pattern cutting (nesting patterns to minimise offcuts, using zero-waste pattern cutting techniques), reducing the number of garments produced, and designing for longevity rather than obsolescence.
  • Reuse — designing products to be used many times (durable, multi-functional, timeless in style) and supporting the second-hand and vintage clothing market. Charity shops, clothing swaps and rental services extend product life before disposal.
  • Recycle — returning textile materials to the raw material stage so they can be used again. Mechanical recycling shreds fabric into fibres that are re-spun into lower-quality yarns (often for insulation or felt). Chemical recycling breaks polymers down to their molecular building blocks, allowing new virgin-quality fibre to be regenerated — currently available for nylon (Econyl) and being developed for polyester and cotton. Post-consumer textile recycling rates remain below 1% globally despite growing collection infrastructure.
  • Rethink — fundamentally questioning the current fast-fashion business model, which encourages consumers to buy more and discard quickly, in favour of circular fashion models where garments are designed, from the outset, to be returned, remanufactured and resold by the brand.
  • Refuse — consumers and designers choosing not to buy or specify products made with particularly harmful materials or under exploitative conditions. Refusing single-use fashion items, non-recyclable synthetic fur or fabrics treated with PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — persistent, bioaccumulative chemicals used in some DWR coatings).
  • Repair — extending the usable life of textile products through mending, darning, patching and remaking. Brands such as Patagonia offer free repair programmes; Japan's boro textile tradition involves repairing and reinforcing old cloth until it becomes a textile of layered patches.
Key Fact

Fast fashion describes the business model of producing large numbers of trend-led garment styles very quickly at low price points, encouraging high-frequency purchasing and rapid disposal. Fast fashion intensifies every sustainability problem in the textile industry: it drives overproduction, increases landfill, worsens microplastic pollution and is associated with poor wages and unsafe working conditions in producing countries.

Sustainable Material Alternatives

Organic cotton is grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilisers, significantly reducing damage to soil ecosystems and farmer health, and using less energy in cultivation. However, organic cotton typically yields 25% less per hectare than conventional cotton, requires more land for the same output, and costs more — factors that limit its adoption despite growing consumer demand. Certification by GOTS (Global Organic Textile Standard) verifies organic status across the whole supply chain from field to finished product.

Recycled polyester (rPET), made from post-consumer plastic bottles or textile waste, uses approximately 59% less energy than virgin polyester and reduces dependence on crude oil. It is now widely used in outdoor clothing, sportswear and fleece. Its limitation is that it still sheds microplastics in the wash and, because recycled fibre is usually a different quality or colour from virgin, blending rPET with virgin polyester is common — making the end garment harder to recycle again.

Lyocell (Tencel) is a manufactured fibre made from wood pulp in a closed-loop solvent process in which 99% of the solvent is recovered and reused. Lyocell is soft, strong, biodegradable and highly absorbent. It drapes like silk and is used in premium casual clothing. Unlike viscose (a similar wood-pulp fibre produced in an open loop with significant chemical discharge), Tencel's production has a much lower environmental impact.

Every time a synthetic fabric garment is washed, it releases hundreds of thousands of microplastic fibres — fragments less than 5 mm in length. These particles pass through most domestic and industrial wastewater treatment systems and enter rivers, lakes and oceans. Marine microplastics are now found in fish, shellfish and drinking water globally. A single wash of a polyester fleece jacket can shed over 700,000 fibres. Mitigation strategies include washing bags (Guppyfriend) that trap shed fibres before they reach the drain, washing machine filters, lower-temperature and shorter wash cycles, and fundamental shifts to natural or biodegradable fibre choices for garments that are washed frequently.

Product and Application Case Study: Performance Sportswear

Modern performance sportswear integrates almost every textile technology covered in this in-depth study. A professional cycling jersey may incorporate: polyester-elastane weft-knit main panels (stretch, moisture wicking, aerodynamic close fit); sublimation printing (vibrant team livery, no surface drag); flatlock overlocked seams (no raised seam ridge to chafe); silicone gripper banding at the hem (holds the jersey in place during a sprint); UV-protective finish (50 UPF rating for long outdoor rides); and recycled polyester construction (brand sustainability messaging).

The choice of each material and construction decision is driven by the performance requirements of the specific sport, the target consumer's willingness to pay (a professional-grade jersey may cost £150–200; a club replica may cost £40), and increasingly by sustainability commitments. No single material or technique provides all the required properties: the garment's performance emerges from the combination of fibre, construction, decoration and finish, all engineered in concert.

Modern Developments in Textile Technology

The textile industry is undergoing rapid technological change. 3D knitting (as used by Nike and Adidas for seamless shoe uppers) builds complete product shapes stitch by stitch from digital files, eliminating cut-and-sew assembly and reducing material waste to near zero. Biofabrication grows leather-like materials from mycelium (fungal root networks) or collagen-producing bacteria, providing animal-free alternatives to leather with a fraction of the carbon footprint. Electrospinning produces nanoscale fibres with very high surface area, useful for filtration, drug delivery membranes and ultra-light insulation. These technologies are moving from laboratory to commercial production but are not yet widely available at mainstream price points.

A circular fashion model aims to keep textiles in use for as long as possible, then return all materials to productive use at end of life with no net waste. Brands such as Patagonia (Worn Wear programme), Eileen Fisher (Renew) and H&M (garment collection points) have established take-back schemes where customers return used garments for resale, reuse or recycling. Challenges include: most garments are blended fibres that are expensive to separate for recycling; returned garments vary enormously in condition; the economics of resale or reprocessing do not yet cover collection costs without subsidy. Legislation such as France's Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires brands to fund collection and recycling infrastructure, is the most effective driver because it internalises costs that were previously externalised to society and the environment.
